name: Excalibur
powers: Blade that cut through any armor; scabbard protected the wearer from wounding.
description: The great sword of King Arthur, given to him by the Lady of the Lake and returned to her waters after his death at Camlann. In Thomas Malory's Le Morte d'Arthur its scabbard protects the wearer from wounding. The name also attaches to the sword Arthur drew from the stone in later romance.

name: Claíomh Mór
powers: Said to bite through any armor or shield.
description: Claíomh Mór, the 'great sword' of Irish tradition, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland and linked with Nuada Airgetlám. Later lore gives it a blade that could pierce any armour or shield. The name is close to, and often confused with, Claíomh Solais, the sword of light.

name: Dyrnwyn
powers: Burst into flame when drawn by a worthy man; burned the unworthy bearer.
description: Dyrnwyn, the sword of Rhydderch Hael, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Drawn by a worthy man it burst into flame; drawn by an unworthy bearer it burned the wielder himself. A noble warrior is said to have taken it, though later tradition preserves few details of its fate.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Gáe Assail
powers: Unstoppable spear of the champion of the Tuatha Dé Danann.
description: Gáe Assail, the great spear of Lugh, one of the four treasures the Tuatha Dé Danann carried into Ireland. Lugh used it at the Second Battle of Mag Tuired, where it helped rout the Fomorians. Its name preserves an older association with the Otherworld gift-bearers of Irish tradition.

name: The Green Knight's Axe
powers: Weapon of the beheading challenge at Camelot.
description: The enormous green-steel axe carried by the Green Knight into King Arthur's hall at the start of the fourteenth-century poem Sir Gawain and the Green Knight. Gawain strikes the Knight's head off with it, and the Knight picks up the severed head, which reminds Gawain of the return blow owed at the Green Chapel.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight (fourteenth century)

name: Durendal
powers: Indestructible blade whose pommel holds relics of Saint Peter, Saint Basil and Saint Denis.
description: Durendal, Roland's sword in the eleventh-century Chanson de Roland. Its gilded pommel holds a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil and hair of Saint Denis. Wounded at Roncevaux, Roland tries to break it against a rock rather than let it fall to the Saracens; the blade survives and the rock splits.

name: Szczerbiec
powers: Symbol of Polish kingship; the notched blade carries the Kiev legend.
description: Szczerbiec, the jagged sword used at Polish coronations from the Middle Ages. Its name, 'the notched one', recalls the legend that Bolesław the Brave struck it against the Golden Gate of Kiev in 1018. The surviving blade, now in Wawel Castle, was damaged in a nineteenth-century theft.

name: Sword of Attila
material: Iron with gold and gem-set hilt
powers: Blade of world dominion pledged to Attila.
description: The sword said to have belonged to Attila the Hun and kept among Hungarian royal treasures. The Roman historian Jordanes records that a shepherd found a blade in the ground that Attila called the Sword of Mars, pledge of world dominion. The gilded iron saber shown in Vienna's Kunsthistorisches Museum is identified with it in later tradition.

name: Tara Brooch
material: Silver-gilt, gold filigree, amber and glass
description: The Tara Brooch, a richly filigreed silver-and-gold annular brooch made around the eighth century. It was discovered in 1850 on the beach at Bettystown, County Meath, and the name 'Tara' was attached for sale because of the site's royal associations. It survives in the National Museum of Ireland with its original chain intact.

name: Great Torc of Snettisham
description: The Great Torc of Snettisham, a necklace of two interlocking gold-alloy rings with ornate buffer terminals, made in eastern England around 75 BC and found in a hoard at Snettisham, Norfolk, in 1950. Such tores marked high status among Iron Age Britons; the example is a centrepiece of the British Museum's Celtic collection.

name: Claddagh Ring
description: The Claddagh, a ring shaped as two hands holding a heart beneath a crown, made in Galway since at least the seventeenth century. The popular story of Richard Joyce, enslaved in Algiers, who sent one home, is late and unverifiable; older written records of the motif are scarce, so the origin legend is treated as tradition rather than fact.

name: Crown of Saint Wenceslas
material: Gold set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds
description: The Crown of Saint Wenceslas, made in 1347 for Charles IV and used to crown Bohemian kings. It is set with rubies, sapphires and emeralds and kept with the other Czech crown jewels. Legend holds that any usurper who sets it on his head will die within a year; it is shown only rarely and under strict conditions.

name: Ship of the Flying Dutchman
powers: Doomed to sail the Cape of Good Hope forever; sighting it is an omen.
description: The ghost ship of the Flying Dutchman, a spectral East Indiaman doomed to round the Cape of Good Hope forever after its captain, variously named Van der Decken, swore against the wind in a storm. Sightings were reported from the seventeenth century onward; no physical vessel exists, and the tale is maritime legend.
source: Maritime legend, from the seventeenth century

name: Prydwen
powers: Arthur's vessel for voyages to the Otherworld stronghold of Annwn.
description: Prydwen, the ship of King Arthur in Welsh tradition. In Culhwch ac Olwen Arthur sails in Prydwen, and the poem Preiddeu Annwn describes Arthur's fleet journey to the Otherworld fortress of Annwn. Welsh sources also give the name to a shield, showing the word shifted between ship and protection.

name: Mantle of Tegau Eurfron
powers: Fitted only a wife faithful to her husband; exposed unfaithful wives.
description: Tegau Eurfron's mantle, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. It would fall only to a wife faithful to her husband; for a woman who had broken her vows it would not cover her, and the truth of her conduct was laid bare. It is the Welsh counterpart of the chastity-testing garments of continental romance.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Arthur's Mantle
powers: Made the wearer invisible while still allowing them to see everything around them.
description: Arthur's mantle, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Whoever wore it became invisible, though the wearer could still see everything about them. The mantle belongs to the Arthur of the medieval Welsh marvel-list tradition, distinct from the later continental Arthur of Malory, and is recorded only in the Welsh treasure catalogue.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Tarnhelm
powers: Rendered the wearer invisible.
description: Tarnhelm, the magic cap of invisibility in the Nibelungenlied. Siegfried takes it from the dwarf Alberich along with the Nibelung hoard; it lets him work unseen. Richard Wagner later gave the name to the golden ring's forging helmet in the Ring cycle, where it also allows shape-shifting, a power absent from the medieval poem.

name: Selkie's Seal-Skin
powers: Lets the selkie shed human form and return to the sea when put back on.
description: The seal-skin of the selkie, the shapeshifting seal-people of Scottish and Irish tradition. A selkie sheds the skin to take human form on land and must have it returned to go back to the sea; a human who hides the skin keeps the selkie as a spouse until the skin is found. The motif underpins the classic selkie-bride tales.

name: Silver Branch of Emain
powers: Its music lulled listeners and summoned heroes to the Otherworld.
description: The silver apple-branch carried by a woman of the Otherworld to the hero Bran in the medieval tale the Voyage of Bran. Its music lulls those who hear it, and Bran leaves with its bearer for the Land of Women across the sea. Messengers of the Irish Otherworld traditionally bear such singing branches.

name: Cormac's Cup
powers: Shattered at a spoken lie and restored itself when truth was told.
description: The cup given to the high king Cormac mac Airt in Echtra Cormaic, offered by a warrior who proves to be Manannán mac Lir. It shatters when a lie is spoken and restores itself when the truth is told, allowing Cormac to test the words of his court. It is one of the moral test-objects of Irish wonder literature.
source: Echtra Cormaic (The Adventure of Cormac mac Airt)

name: Frau Holle's Feather Bed
powers: Shaken by Frau Holle, its feathers fall to earth as snow.
description: Frau Holle's feather bed, the great bedding the old woman shakes in the Grimm tale of the same name. Each time she shakes it the feathers fall as snow, which is why, the tale explains, snow falls in winter. The heroine earns it through service; the episode is the story's comic explanation of the seasons.

name: Franks Casket
description: The Franks Casket, an eighth-century Anglo-Saxon chest carved from whalebone, covered with scenes from Germanic legend, the Bible and classical history, with runic and Latin inscriptions. The front panel shows the smith Weland being released by a maiden he rescued. It was bought in the nineteenth century and is now in the British Museum.

name: Cauldron of Rebirth
powers: Restored slain warriors to life, though the revived could not speak.
description: Pair Dadeni, the Cauldron of Rebirth in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi. Given to Brân the Blessed by a giant couple from Ireland, it restores slain warriors to life, though the revived cannot speak. In the war for Branwen the cauldron is finally shattered by Efnysien, who throws himself into it.

name: Cauldron of the Dagda
powers: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied.
description: Coire an Dagda, the Dagda's cauldron, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. It is the cauldron of plenty: no company ever went away from it unsatisfied. With the spear of Lugh, the stone of Fal and the sword of Nuada it ranks among the wonder-gifts carried into Ireland by the Old Gods.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann

name: Lia Fáil
powers: Cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it.
description: Lia Fáil, the Stone of Destiny at the hill of Tara, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. In tradition it cried out beneath the rightful king of Ireland when he stood on it. The medieval account of the coronation of Conn is the best-known instance of the stone's voice.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; Baile in Scáil

name: Ardagh Chalice
material: Silver, bronze, gold filigree, glass and enamel
description: The Ardagh Chalice, a silver-and-bronze liturgical cup made around the eighth century, found in 1868 in a ring-fort at Ardagh, County Limerick, with a hoard of other church metalwork. Its decorated panels of gold filigree, glass and enamel mark it as a masterpiece of Insular art; it is held by the National Museum of Ireland.

name: The Grail of Peredur
description: The dish or salver carried in the procession at the castle of Peredur in the medieval Welsh romance that bears his name. Unlike the French Grail romances, the Welsh text describes a bleeding head on a salver and a woman carrying a dish, a version that preserves a distinct Celtic Arthurian strand. The item is legendary and unattested.

name: Nanteos Cup
description: The Nanteos Cup, a late medieval wooden mazer bowl kept for two centuries at Nanteos mansion in Ceredigion and treated as a healing cup. Sick pilgrims were said to drink from it, and its gradual erosion was blamed on those who bit or scraped it. Claims that it was the Holy Grail began only in the nineteenth century and remain unverified.

name: Ceridwen's Cauldron
powers: Brewed the Awen, the drops of inspiration and knowledge, for a year and a day.
description: Ceridwen's cauldron in the medieval Tale of Taliesin, in which the goddess-figure Ceridwen brews a potion of inspiration for her son for a year and a day. The three drops fall on Gwion, who swallows them and gains the Awen before being transformed and pursued through animal shapes. The cauldron is wholly legendary.

name: Pied Piper's Pipe
powers: Its music charmed rats, and later children, following the piper out of Hamelin.
description: The pipe of the Pied Piper of Hamelin, the instrument whose music lured the town's rats to the river Weser, and then, when the townsfolk refused payment, drew the children away into a mountainside. No actual pipe survives; it belongs to the semi-legendary 1284 Hamelin tradition and its later retellings.
source: Hamelin tradition; Grimm and Browning retellings

name: Green Knight's Holly Branch
description: The holly branch carried by the Green Knight in Sir Gawain and the Green Knight when he rides unarmed into Arthur's hall. Its evergreen branches mark him as one of the winter gods of the older year, and he uses it to hold his own axe as he delivers his challenge. It is an emblem of the poem's beheading-game and seasonal cycle.
source: Sir Gawain and the Green Knight

name: The Round Table
powers: Seated all the knights of Arthur's court without quarrels over precedence.
description: The Round Table of King Arthur, the great table at which none of the knights could claim a higher seat than another. In Geoffrey of Monmouth it is a table of guests; in later romance the table, like Arthur's court, is divided when Merlin reads the fate of a knight who will win the Grail. A 13th-century table at Winchester is linked to the legend.
source: Geoffrey of Monmouth; Arthurian romance; Winchester table

name: The Singing Harp
powers: Sang on its own and cried out for its master, waking the giant.
description: The singing golden harp of the giant in the tale of Jack and the Beanstalk. As Jack climbs down the beanstalk with the hen and the gold, the harp calls out for its master, waking the giant and setting the chase in motion. It is one of the three treasures the giant keeps in his castle.
source: Jack and the Beanstalk (English fairy tale)

name: The Magic Mirror
powers: Told its owner who was the fairest in the land.
description: The magic mirror of the queen in the Grimm tale of Snow White. Each time she asks 'Mirror, mirror on the wall, who is the fairest of them all?', the mirror answers truly, and its answer drives the queen to send Snow White into the wood. The mirror is a test-object of the tale and exists only in fiction.

name: Cinderella's Glass Slipper
powers: Fitted only Cinderella, letting the prince find her after the ball.
description: The glass slipper in the Grimms' Aschenputtel, the shoe lost as Cinderella flees the prince's ball. Because it fits no other foot in the kingdom, it lets the prince find his bride. Perrault's version makes the slipper glass; the object is a fairy-tale token and no such slipper survives.
source: Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen no. 21; Perrault

name: The Six Swans' Shirts
powers: Thrown over her swan brothers, restored them to human form.
description: The six shirts of stinging nettles woven in silence by the sister in the Grimms' tale of the six swans. For years she must sew them without speaking a word; when at last they are thrown over her brothers, the swans become men again. The shirt-making is the tale's central task and ordeal.

name: Briar Rose's Spinning Wheel
powers: Pricked the princess and cast the whole castle into a hundred-year sleep.
description: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' Dornröschen, whose spindle pricks the sleeping princess and sends the entire castle into a century of sleep. The king had ordered all spindles burned, but the old woman in the tower still spins. When the prince cuts through the thorns, the spindle's pricking is undone and the wheel stands still.

name: The Golden Goose
powers: Stuck fast anyone who touched it, drawing a growing chain of followers.
description: Die goldene Gans, the goose from the Grimms' tale of the same name. Found by Dummling in the wood, the golden goose sticks fast to anyone who touches it, so that the whole town follows in a chain behind him; the sight makes the sad princess laugh, winning her hand. The goose is a purely fictional marvel.

name: The Papyrus of Ani
aliases: Book of the Dead of Ani
maker: Scribes of Thebes for the scribe Ani
powers: Guides the deceased through the judgment of the afterlife.
description: The finest surviving Book of the Dead manuscript, commissioned for the Theban scribe Ani around 1250 BCE. Its long roll of vignettes and hieroglyphic spells was meant to guide the dead through the afterlife, most famously the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma'at in chapter 125, with Ani and his wife shown before the gods. It is the classic witness to Egyptian funerary literature.
source: The Book of the Dead (Papyrus of Ani), British Museum EA 10470

name: Eye of Horus
powers: Protects the wearer and restores wholeness; the healed eye of the falcon god.
description: The wedjat, the eye that the god Thoth healed after Set tore it from Horus, worn as an amulet of protection, healing, and wholeness. Its hieroglyphic fractions were used for measuring grain volumes, and thousands of wedjat amulets in faience, gold, and stone survive in tombs from the Old Kingdom into the Graeco-Roman period, where the sign still guarded the living and the dead.
source: Egyptian amulets and temple reliefs; Pyramid Texts
